section.title: Computer algebra systems and integral tables
section.p: A computer algebra system can differentiate, integrate, simplify, factor, expand, and solve equations. An integral table can list thousands of antiderivative patterns.
These tools are useful. They are also dangerous when used passively.

A tool may give an answer that is correct on one interval but not another. It may return an expression that looks different from yours. It may use a special function you have not seen before. It may hide an absolute value. It may even produce a form that is harder to understand than the original problem.
section.md: \text{Use tools to check and explore, not to surrender judgment.}

subsection.title: A responsible workflow with tools
subsection.p: When using a table or computer algebra system, work in this order.

row.cell: Step
Action
Inspect the integrand first. Identify possible structure.
Try a human method if the structure is clear.
Use a table or CAS to check, compare, or explore.
Differentiate the returned antiderivative.
Check the interval, branch, and absolute values.
For a definite integral, check whether endpoints or discontinuities cause trouble.
Decide whether an exact form, special-function form, or decimal approximation is most useful.

subsection.p: The last endpoint check points toward the next section. A definite integral over a finite interval with a continuous integrand is safe. But many important integrals are not of that kind. The interval may be infinite. The integrand may blow up. A formal antiderivative may exist while the accumulated amount is not finite.
